planting.note: Divide and repot clumps into fresh fine bark or sphagnum right after flowering and once night temperatures are reliably above 45F; this high-elevation Peruvian species is a greenhouse or cool-room subject outside true cloud-forest climates.

directions: Pot this Peruvian cloud-forest miniature in a small basket or clay pot of fine fir bark and live sphagnum so roots stay evenly moist but never waterlogged. Keep nights cool, around 50-58F, with constant high humidity and steady air movement to prevent crown rot. Waxy cream-to-pale-yellow flowers with fine purple-maroon spotting are borne singly on short stems close to the foliage through cooler months. Avoid any direct sun; dappled greenhouse shade or an east-facing windowsill under sheer curtain is ideal.

planting.note: Best divided and mounted or repotted in spring as new growth starts; grow year-round in a cool, shaded greenhouse or terrarium since this Andean species has no dormancy and dislikes warm, dry rooms.

directions: This small Ecuadorian and Peruvian Andean species gets its common name from an unusually long, narrow, fringed lip that projects from the yellow-and-maroon flower like an extended tongue. Grow mounted on tree-fern or in a shallow pot of fine bark and sphagnum, kept constantly moist with cool nights in the 50s. Strong, steady air movement and bright open shade mimic its native cloud-forest understory and help prevent fungal spotting on the thin leaves. Flowers are produced individually on wiry stems and can appear at almost any time of year under stable conditions.

planting.note: Grow permanently in a slotted basket hung where pendent flower spikes can drop freely below the pot rim; repot/divide in spring once temperatures stabilize above 45F at night.

directions: One of the most famous Dracula species, this Colombian cloud-forest orchid produces large triangular flowers heavily mottled in maroon and cream on long pendent stems, so it must be grown in a hanging slotted basket that lets spikes trail downward beneath the plant. Pot in an open mix of coarse bark and sphagnum, keep constantly moist, and hold night temperatures in the 50s with bright, even shade year-round. The flowers carry a faint mushroom-like scent that attracts the fungus-gnat pollinators they mimic in shape and markings. It resents heat and drying out, so steady cool humidity is essential rather than optional.

planting.note: Keep permanently in a hanging slotted basket so pendent spikes can emerge from the bottom; divide only when the basket is overcrowded, ideally in spring.

directions: Native to high-elevation cloud forests on the Colombia-Ecuador border, this species produces some of the largest flowers in the genus, cream to tan with heavy brown mottling and long tapering sepal tails. Because flower spikes emerge from the base and hang downward, plants need a slotted or open-sided basket raised well above eye level. Keep the fine bark-and-sphagnum mix constantly damp, nights cool in the 50s, and humidity high with good airflow to avoid rot. It is slower growing and less common in collections than some other Dracula species but equally dependent on stable cool, shaded conditions.

planting.note: Divide mats of growths in spring into small clumps rather than single stems, which establish faster in fresh fine bark or mounted on cork.

directions: Ranging from Mexico to Venezuela, this creeping miniature forms dense mats of small single leaves with wiry flower stems bearing blooms marked in fine reddish-brown streaks and spots that resemble resting flies. It tolerates intermediate as well as cool temperatures, making it more forgiving than many Andean miniatures, but still wants constant moisture and bright shade rather than direct sun. Mount on a cork or tree-fern slab, or pot shallowly in fine bark with sphagnum, and mist or water frequently so the thin roots never fully dry. Established mats flower repeatedly through the year rather than in a single flush.

planting.note: Divide creeping growths in spring, keeping several leaves per division, and reattach to a mount or shallow pot immediately so roots do not dry out.

directions: Found from Trinidad into northern South America, this small creeping species carries single flowers with a distinctly twisted, narrow lip held beneath flat paired sepals striped in maroon on a pale ground. It grows well mounted on cork or in a shallow basket of fine bark and sphagnum under bright, even shade with cool to intermediate night temperatures. Constant humidity and light misting keep the thin fibrous roots active, since the plant has no pseudobulbs to store water. Like other Restrepia it spreads as a creeping mat and is best left undisturbed for several seasons between repottings.

planting.note: Divide clumps of upright stems in spring and reset into fresh fine bark mix promptly, since the fine roots have little tolerance for drying between repots.

directions: Named for its resemblance to Restrepia, this small Central American species carries single leaves on short upright stems and produces slender, pale flowers streaked with fine reddish veining at the leaf base. It comes from mid-elevation cloud forest and grows best in a small pot of fine bark and sphagnum kept evenly moist, with bright shade and cool-to-intermediate night temperatures. Good air circulation around the clumping stems is important to prevent the thin leaves from spotting in constantly damp conditions. It is a lesser-grown species outside specialist Pleurothallis collections but well documented in cloud-forest orchid surveys.
